arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Thompson argued the categorical method requires strict reliance on statutory elements.
She contended ambiguous convictions obtained under nongeneric statutes cannot be used as predicates.
Mr. Elwood argued police reports help clarify the specific property involved in the crime.
He stated the Court can look to conviction records to determine predicate status.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Shepard v. United States tests the limits of the categorical method. This approach requires courts to look only at the statutory elements of a prior conviction. The case asks if courts may examine supporting documents when a statute covers multiple types of property.

The government wants the conviction counted as a qualifying predicate offense.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues courts must ignore police reports and rely solely on statutory text.
The government argues police reports provide necessary context for ambiguous statutes.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice O'Connor asked if supporting documents show the property was a building, car, or boat.
Justice Scalia asked for a definition of a nongeneric burglary statute.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines how federal courts interpret state criminal records. It determines whether judges can use police reports to clarify ambiguous convictions. This process affects federal sentencing calculations for career criminals. It impacts the consistency of federal sentencing guidelines nationwide.
